article_text:
È il 1964 quando Pier Paolo Pasolini , durante le riprese de Il Vangelo secondo Matteo , scopre il paesaggio di Chia, nel Viterbese . Tra boschi, cascate e rovine medievali, rimane folgorato da una torre che domina la valle del Fosso Castello. Nel 1970 decide di acquistarla, trasformandola nel proprio rifugio intellettuale ed esistenziale, lontano dall’Italia dell’omologazione che avrebbe denunciato nei suoi scritti.

Nel 2021 la proprietà viene acquistata dall’attore Gabriele Gallinari , che vende la propria abitazione a Roma per trasferirsi stabilmente alla Torre, facendone la sua residenza principale. Qui intraprende importanti interventi di recupero e manutenzione, investendo risorse personali nella conservazione del complesso e restituendo vita a un luogo profondamente legato alla memoria dello scrittore.

Ma nel 2025 una sentenza del Commissario agli usi civici, discostandosi totalmente dalle conclusioni del Consulente Tecnico d’Ufficio, accoglie le rivendicazioni dell’Università Agraria di Chia, ente privato con 120 iscritti. Riconosce la natura demaniale civica dei terreni interessati, dichiara la nullità della compravendita e ne dispone la reintegrazione nel patrimonio civico, senza prevedere la corresponsione di alcun indennizzo economico all’attuale proprietario, nonostante le somme investite in buona fede nell’acquisto e nel recupero del complesso.

Si apre così una controversia tra un privato cittadino, che sostiene di avere acquistato legittimamente la proprietà e di averne finanziato il recupero, e un ente privato che ne rivendica la titolarità sulla base degli usi civici sino a quel momento non manifesti. Gallinari ha fatto ricorso alla Corte d’Appello, nel 2028 la decisione. Ma nel frattempo la sentenza del 7 aprile 2025 è esecutiva e la Regione Lazio ha avviato la procedura di rilascio, benché il giudizio d’appello sia ancora pendente. I 30 giorni concessi per il rilascio sono scaduti e il proprietario ha presentato ricorso al TAR contro il provvedimento regionale.

Per Gallinari si tratta, nei fatti, di un esproprio senza indennizzo; per l’Università Agraria, dell’acquisizione di un bene che ritiene appartenere al patrimonio civico. Una distinzione giuridica sostanziale, dietro la quale emerge una questione culturale più ampia: a chi appartiene la memoria di un luogo e chi ha il diritto, o il dovere, di custodirla? Ne parliamo con Gabriele Gallinari, per ricostruire quanto sta accadendo e riflettere sul rapporto tra proprietà privata, interesse pubblico e tutela del patrimonio culturale.

Pasolini riconobbe a Chia qualcosa che l’Italia stava perdendo: il silenzio, il paesaggio e una particolare forma di libertà. Che cosa ha riconosciuto lei in quella torre quando ha deciso di acquistarla?

«Il primo incontro con questo luogo è stato, prima di tutto, un’esperienza di spaesamento. Varcato il cancello, ci si trova davanti a un paesaggio dominato dai ruderi, nel quale persino la presenza delle abitazioni risulta inizialmente impercettibile, quasi fossero state deliberatamente sottratte allo sguardo. La sensazione è quella di aver sbagliato destinazione, oppure di essere entrati in una dimensione temporale estranea alla contemporaneità.

È stata proprio questa sospensione, insieme alla straordinaria integrità del contesto naturale, a esercitare su di me il fascino più profondo. Soltanto in un secondo momento, entrando negli ambienti realizzati da Pasolini, si comprende la singolarità dell’intervento architettonico.

Non si trattò, infatti, di un semplice restauro: Pasolini fece costruire nuovi edifici su progetto di Dante Ferretti , introducendo nel paesaggio medievale un linguaggio architettonico sorprendentemente moderno, che richiama certe esperienze californiane degli anni Quaranta. Ne deriva una sorta di cortocircuito spazio-temporale, nel quale epoche apparentemente inconciliabili trovano un equilibrio inatteso. Il legno, la pietra e il vetro stabiliscono un rapporto di continuità con l’ambiente circostante, senza mai pretendere di dominarlo.

Si avverte costantemente la possibilità che la natura torni a riappropriarsi di quegli spazi. Pasolini la chiamava «casa luce»: una definizione che restituisce efficacemente il senso di un’architettura concepita non come imposizione sul paesaggio, ma come luogo di relazione tra memoria e modernità».

Lei ha restituito vita a un luogo carico di memoria e oggi rischia di perderlo. Non è singolare che proprio chi investe nella conservazione di un patrimonio si ritrovi privato della sua custodia?

«È precisamente questa la contraddizione più profonda, e per certi aspetti più difficile da accettare, dell’intera vicenda. Quando ho acquistato la proprietà, il complesso versava in condizioni di sostanziale abbandono e non sembrava suscitare alcun concreto interesse né da parte delle Istituzioni né da parte di altri privati. Ho ritenuto che un luogo di tale rilevanza storica, culturale e paesaggistica non potesse essere lasciato al proprio deterioramento. È stata una scelta consapevole, che ha comportato un investimento personale considerevole: per rendere possibile il recupero ho venduto persino la mia prima casa a Roma.

Non si è trattato di un’operazione speculativa, ma di un progetto di conservazione e restituzione alla vita di un patrimonio che rischiava di scomparire. L’acquisto è avvenuto attraverso procedure regolari e sulla base delle verifiche effettuate nelle sedi competenti. Il Comune aveva rilasciato una certificazione attestante l’assenza di usi civici, lo Stato non aveva esercitato il diritto di prelazione e persino un’interrogazione parlamentare ha affrontato la questione della natura privata della proprietà.

Ho sostenuto integralmente i costi dell’intervento, senza ricorrere a finanziamenti del PNRR o a specifici contributi pubblici. Il restauro, durato tre anni e mezzo, è stato condotto sotto la supervisione della Soprintendenza, nel rispetto del valore storico e architettonico del complesso. Dal primo giorno ho voluto che il sito fosse accessibile ai visitatori, attraverso una convenzione con il Comune di Soriano nel Cimino, Enti Ministeriali ed eventi culturali a titolo gratuito.

Trovo dunque paradossale che un’iniziativa privata, capace di recuperare un bene abbandonato e di renderlo fruibile alla collettività, possa oggi tradursi nel rischio di perdere proprio quel patrimonio che si è riusciti a salvaguardare. La tutela, a mio avviso, dovrebbe riconoscere e valorizzare chi si assume concretamente la responsabilità della conservazione, non trasformare tale impegno in una condizione di vulnerabilità».

Pasolini fece della torre un luogo di libertà e di ricerca intellettuale. Quali prospettive immagina per questo patrimonio e in che modo sarebbe possibile restituirlo alla collettività senza comprometterne l’identità e la memoria?

«Avevo già aperto questo luogo alla collettività. Gli sconvolgimenti attuali piuttosto mettono a rischio il futuro di questo patrimonio culturale. Le prospettive non sono rassicuranti. È complicato in questo momento immaginare ciò che sarà, ma se torno alle ragioni che mi hanno spinto ad acquistare la torre, ritrovo una convinzione che non è mai venuta meno: questo luogo deve essere conservato, vissuto e condiviso.

Qualora l’esito del procedimento giudiziario mi fosse favorevole, vorrei semplicemente proseguire il percorso intrapreso. La Torre di Chia non è un patrimonio sottratto alla collettività: è già accessibile al pubblico, proprio in virtù di una scelta che ho compiuto volontariamente. Per questo considero profondamente discutibile il ricorso alla nozione di “interesse pubblico” per giustificare un eventuale esproprio senza indennizzo.

Occorrerebbe innanzitutto interrogarsi su che cosa si intenda realmente con questa espressione e su quali soggetti ne sarebbero gli effettivi beneficiari. Non è sufficiente invocare la collettività quando, nella pratica, l’interesse potrebbe riguardare una cerchia circoscritta di iscritti a un ente privato, mentre la generalità dei visitatori continuerebbe ad accedere al sito attraverso un regolare biglietto d’ingresso.

Il complesso è stato restaurato, è sottoposto alla tutela della Soprintendenza ed è inserito in un sistema di fruizione pubblica già funzionante. Quale sarebbe, dunque, l’urgenza di sottrarlo a chi ne garantisce la conservazione, per di più prima che la controversia abbia trovato una definizione giudiziaria definitiva?

Ritengo che l’eventualità di un’acquisizione a titolo gratuito sollevi interrogativi estremamente seri, non soltanto sul piano del diritto di proprietà, ma anche su quello della certezza giuridica e della fiducia dei cittadini nelle istituzioni. La memoria di Pasolini merita certamente una tutela rigorosa, ma non credo che questa debba necessariamente coincidere con il trasferimento della proprietà.

La dimensione pubblica di un bene culturale non dipende esclusivamente da chi lo possiede, bensì dalla qualità della sua conservazione, dalla possibilità di conoscerlo e dalla responsabilità con cui viene tramandato, principi questi già garantiti dal vincolo dei Beni Culturali. Ed è su questi princìpi, credo, che dovrebbe fondarsi qualsiasi riflessione sul futuro della Torre di Chia».

article_text:
Opinion

Dear Art World, We Can Tell When You’re Using AI

Institutions, especially well-resourced museums, foundations, and cultural organizations, have no excuse for relying on generative tools instead of paying writers.

Hyperallergic ; video Getty Images, photo public domain via

Wikimedia Commons )

Wall labels. Press releases. Artist statements. In today’s fast-paced art world, the written word stands at a crucial crossroads — and the stakes have never been higher. But here’s the thing: It’s not just about convenience. It’s about authenticity. Because the way we express ourselves matters.

The above paragraph was generated by Claude when prompted to write an introduction for an opinion piece against AI use in art writing, and if it made you recoil in your seat, you may be among those of us who have developed a strong aversion to generative text. You’ll know it when you see it: that uncanny cadence that’s overconfident in style yet hollow in substance, like a motivational LinkedIn post that feels relatable at first but leaves you with as much nourishment as a spoonful of Stevia.

People like me, who read, write, and edit words for a living, are perhaps more attuned to the artificial staccato and mawkish pathos of generative text. Still, its growing pervasiveness in the so-called “art world” (the sphere of museums, galleries, fairs, et al.) is undeniable. As an artist friend who recently DM’d me an obviously AI-drafted press release from a well-respected Manhattan institution put it: “Wow, they really have no shame.”

As an editor at Hyperallergic , a publication that has centered the lived experience of artists since its very inception, I am sensitive to the time- and resource-intensive nature of producing written material. The burden of self-promotion placed on artists and cultural workers has become untenable, particularly for those without a gallery or assistant to outsource such tasks to. Artists are spending precious time out of the studio drafting exhibition texts, lengthy grant applications , or social media copy for the online presence that is increasingly expected of them, often with little training and no compensation. It is no surprise that when tools emerge to optimize these duties, creative people will flock to them, not because they do not value the work of writers but because they wish to protect their own artistic labor.

Institutions, on the other hand, especially well-resourced museums, foundations, publications, and other cultural organizations, have no excuse for relying on artificial intelligence for textual materials (and underpaid, overworked museum workers must be given more time and resources to avoid the temptation of delegating original writing to AI). I would also add to that list PR representatives, marketing professionals, or anyone else whose principal responsibility is to communicate adeptly with the public and members of the press. Needless to say, journalists and other writers — who unfortunately face similar conditions of precarity as artists — have a moral responsibility to uphold the integrity of our profession by keeping AI out of the heart of the writing process: crafting original sentences whose form deepens their substance. As Wired elegantly puts it in its own AI guidelines : “We think someone who writes for a living needs to constantly be thinking about the best way to express complex ideas in their own words."
excerpt_original: Institutions, especially well-resourced museums, foundations, and cultural organizations, have no excuse for relying on generative tools instead of paying writers.

"霍什达斯特在拍摄对象时曾不止一次冒着被捕的风险，他表示，捕捉拍摄对象生存的最基本状态至关重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他表示，赢得他们的信任“大约花了2年时间，或许稍微少一点，但分成了3个不同的阶段。我已经熟悉了他们的生活，并理解了他们日常琐事的重复循环。我决定将这3个阶段拍摄的素材汇集在一起，作为电影开篇的3个片段，从而给人一种一切都发生在短短1到2天内的错觉，就像有3个摄制组在同时拍摄一样。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“正是在那时，我们遇到了哈米德和他的家人。我向他讲述了我自己的生活以及我所遭受的伊斯兰革命卫队的迫害。哈米德问我：‘如果我把我的故事告诉你，你会把它写下来吗？’我回答说：‘碰巧我是个纪录片导演，我想为你拍一部电影。’他们后来邀请我们去他们家里，一切开始朝着我作为导演所希望的方向发展。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，哈米德的家人分享了他们在面对工作许可令人发指的拖延，同时又被迫打黑工时所经历的精疲力竭、创伤与困惑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与此同时，由于警察的关注构成了持续的威胁，一种偏执感也随之滋生。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "霍什达斯特解释说：“我们在3个地点进行了拍摄：作为我们主要拍摄地的安卡拉、哈娜内工作的阿拉尼亚，以及哈米德工作的一座靠近伊斯坦布尔的工业城镇。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当时的环境极其紧张且令人恐惧。我们被拘留了2到3次。最严重的一次事件发生在安卡拉，那是在一次恐怖袭击之后的一段时间。一天晚上，在拍摄完一场电梯戏份后，警官们来到哈米德的家，企图拘留我。朋友们当晚出面干预，并保证我第二天会去警察局报到。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“还有一次，一名土耳其公民谎报称我们一直在拍摄埃尔多安总统的家！当我被拘留时，我以为自己要心脏病发作了。我曾拍过伊朗监狱内部的画面并在那里被捕过，但这完全是另一回事。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着人们越来越担心哈米德及其家人可能受到监视，他们的故事变得更加复杂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "导演说，这展现了多达50万被迫逃离祖国的伊朗人可能正在经历的遭遇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他说：“但对我和艺术家来说，哪怕只有一家人陷入这种境遇，也是多了一家人。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“对于像土耳其这样的国家的伊朗人来说，抑郁和思乡之情可能会特别严重。他们已经离开了祖国，但在某种程度上，他们并没有真正开始在其他地方的新生活。他们依然处于游离状态。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“许多人最终一无所有地回了家。但哈米德和他的儿子永远无法回去。哈米德在艰难地坚持，但他别无选择。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "导演说，这位父亲的旅程具有双重的辛酸，因为当他意识到自己的技术专长正被用于该国的导弹系统时，他选择离开在伊朗的前途无量的职业生涯。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“曾有一个伊朗人对我说，如果哈米德留在伊朗并同意从事导弹发射器的工作，他现在就会很富有，手下有一整支团队为他工作。如果他在欧洲或美国，他本可以成为一名杰出的工程师。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“相反，他在土耳其过着游牧般的不稳定生活，因为没有人支持他。最近，他告诉我说，他甚至连开银行账户的资格都没有。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "导演质问：“究竟是什么样的世界，会让这样的天才白白浪费，而所有人却只是在一旁冷眼旁观？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "霍什达斯特在拍摄过程中发现，拍摄对象的精神负担往往重得令人难以承受——正因如此，他选择始终与一位摄影师合作，以便自己能贴近他们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“有时他们在我的怀里哭泣。我会抱抱他们，安慰他们，然后引导他们走到镜头前，确保他们既看不到摄影师，也感受不到他的存在。我还必须为我的摄影师做好准备，以这种方式工作。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "霍什达斯特说，这种方法是他在拍摄上一部纪录片《红线深处》时发展起来的，该片聚焦服刑的年轻人，合作对象是莫尔特扎·普尔萨马迪（Morteza Poursamadi），“我认为他是伊朗纪录片电影史上最伟大的摄影师”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "导演说，《第三片土地》的诞生是因为“我和妻子把所有的积蓄都花在了这部电影的制作和拍摄上。拍完后，我们身无分文。更糟糕的是，伊朗的安全形势意味着我无法回去”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如今，这种身份也成了他和银幕上那些饱受挣扎的家庭所共同的经历。", "translated": true}, {"type": article_text:
In the unnerving docu “Third Land,” director and Iranian émigré Farzad Khoshdast chronicles the permanent limbo of a family living on the margins in Turkey.

Screening at the Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival this week, the film follows an Iranian engineer, his wife, Hananeh, and son as they deal with the daily contradictions of life as refugees in a third land – that is, one where their refugee status has been recognized by international aid organizations but their legal residence has not been.

Related Stories

Taylor Swift's 'Patient Zero' Holds Steady at No. 1 for Second Week on Singles Chart

Khoshdast, who more than once risked arrest while filming his subjects, says he felt it was essential to capture the bare bones of his subjects’ existence.

Gaining their trust, he says, took “around two years, perhaps a little less, but across three distinct periods. I had become familiar with their lives and understood the repetitive cycle of their daily routines. I decided to bring together footage shot during those three periods as the film’s opening three episodes, creating the impression that everything was happening over just one or two days, as though three crews had been filming simultaneously.”

He calls this approach to storytelling, and the way it brings different periods of time together, “one of the film’s important structural features.”

Khoshdast and his wife were traveling in Turkey about four years ago, he says.

“That was when we met Hamid and his family. I told him about my own life and the harm I had suffered at the hands of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Hamid asked me, ‘If I tell you my story, will you write it down?’ I replied, ‘As it happens, I’m a documentary filmmaker, and I’d like to make a film about you.’ They later invited us into their home, and everything began to take the shape I had hoped for as a filmmaker.”

Indeed, Hamid’s family shares the exhaustion, trauma and confusion they experience as they face maddening delays in getting work permits while forced to find employment under the table.

Meanwhile, a sense of paranoia grows as police interest represents a constant threat.

“We filmed in three locations: Ankara, our main location; Alanya, where Hananeh worked; and an industrial town near Istanbul, where Hamid worked,” Khoshdast explains.

“The circumstances were extremely tense and frightening. We were detained two or three times. The most serious incident happened in Ankara, some time after a terrorist attack. One night, following the filming of an elevator scene, officers came to Hamid’s home intending to detain me. Friends intervened that night and gave assurances that I would report to the police station the following day.”

“On another occasion, a Turkish citizen falsely reported that we had been filming President Erdoğan’s home! When I was detained, I thought I was going to have a heart attack. I had filmed inside prisons in Iran and had been arrested there, but this was something else entirely.”

As worries grew that Hamid and his family might be under surveillance, their story became still more complicated.

It illustrates what may be happening to as many as half a million Iranians who have been forced to flee their home country, the director says.

“But for me, as an artist,” he says, “even one family trapped in such circumstances is one family too many.”

“Depression and homesickness can be particularly severe for Iranians in countries such as Turkey. They have left their homeland, yet in a sense they have not truly been able to begin a new life elsewhere. They remain in limbo.”

“Many eventually return home with nothing. But Hamid and his son can never return. Hamid struggles to carry on, but he has no other choice.”

This father’s journey is doubly poignant, the director says, because he chose to leave a promising career in Iran once he realized his technical skills were being used as part of the country’s missile system.

“An Iranian once told me that if Hamid had stayed in Iran and agreed to work on missile launchers, he would now be wealthy, with an entire staff working for him. Had he been in Europe or the United States, he would have become an outstanding engineer.”

“Instead, he lives a nomadic, precarious existence in Turkey because nobody supports him. Recently, he told me he is not even permitted to have a bank account.”

“What kind of world allows such talent to go to waste while everyone simply watches?” the director asks.

Khoshdast found while shooting that his subjects’ emotional burdens are often overwhelming – so much so that he chooses to work with a cinematographer at all times so that he himself can remain close to them.

“Sometimes they cried in my arms. I would hold them, comfort them, and then guide them in front of the camera, making sure they neither saw the cinematographer nor felt his presence. I also had to prepare my cinematographer to work in this way.”

Khoshdast developed the approach, he says, while working on his previous docu, “Narrow Red Line,” which follows young people incarcerated, working with Morteza Poursamadi, “whom I consider the greatest cinematographer in the history of Iranian documentary cinema.”

“Third Land” came about, the director says, because “my wife and I spent all our savings on the film’s production and shooting. When it was over, we had no money left. Worse still, the security situation in Iran meant I could not return.”

That status he now shares with the family whose struggles unfold onscreen.

“Third Land” screens in the Czech Joy section of the Ji.hlava fest, running through Nov. 1.

article_text:
Writer-director Bassam Tariq ‘s “ Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother ” is one of those rare movies that doesn’t feel like anything you’ve seen before. That’s partly due to the unusual blend of tones in its premise — a devout Muslim family man ( Mahershala Ali ) is also a contract killer whose religion and job are in serious conflict — and partly due to its depiction of a group of people (practicing Muslims living in Houston, Texas) who don’t normally get their stories told on American movie screens.

Both of these factors had to be taken into consideration by costume designer Deirdra Elizabeth Govan, who meticulously researched the faith and culture at the center of the film to tell a detailed story through the characters’ clothing. One aspect of the story came naturally to Govan, however. “I was born and raised in Houston, Texas,” Govan told IndieWire. “Reading the script, I really appreciated Bassam’s capacity for understanding how diverse Texas is, and Houston specifically.”

When it came to Latif, the main character played by Mahershala Ali , Govan knew she had to embrace the character’s contradictions. “This is a man who is battling his faith,” Govan said. “I wanted to be very mindful and respectful of Muslim identity, but not fall into a prescribed idea of what a Muslim is, because there is no such thing. But there is a construct of Black Muslim style and contemporary modern life, an unabashed way of dress that is vibrant, that is rich in texture, that is rich in color and swag.”

Govan drew upon a wide array of influences for Latif’s clothes, referencing Tuareg (particularly in the indigo color palette) and Baye Fall African warriors, as well as the more utilitarian aspects of Japanese samurai clothing. “I had to maintain a balance, because this character’s everyday life is as a father,” Govan said, “but when we first meet him we’re introduced to him as a killer. We don’t know his backstory. So there’s a level of restraint that’s very important — I didn’t want the costumes to announce themselves.”

Several of Latif’s costumes were original designs Govan created to reflect his daily life and emotional state. “For the funeral scene, I designed his thobe to combine a traditional tunic silhouette with the details of a tailored men’s dress shirt: micro-stripe shirting with a contrasting denim band collar and cuffs. I also designed the loose shalwar trousers in blue and white that he wears during his meditative practice with his sword. His multicolored morning tunic, with its long sleeves, reflects his attempt at optimism. Across these looks, the untucked shirts, long sleeves, and loose trousers maintain the modesty and ease that ground his everyday looks, while the individual details express different aspects of his character.”

Latif’s duality becomes especially clear in his long denim kimono coat, which Govan created in collaboration with Daisuke Muramatsu, owner of Prospective Flow, using pieces from his collection. “It brings the warrior influences of my research into Latif’s contemporary assassin look while remaining rooted in his everyday wardrobe,” Govan said. “The addition of his Tuareg-inspired tagelmust and the embossed leather belt holding his sword sheath changes its function and how we read him. Latif remains a father, a man of faith, and a warrior throughout that seamless transition.”

While Latif represents one approach to faith and violence, his adversary Pastor Hwan (John Cho) represents another. An evangelist cult leader in charge of a heavily armed militia, Hwan is as sincere in his beliefs as Latif is in his — and seems completely unaware of the even greater contradictions between his faith as he preaches it and his actions in practice. “My research really began with cult leaders and how they are able to draw people in,” Govan said. “How do they identify in their dress and style?”

In addition to real-life cult and religious leaders, Govan was influenced by the look of the John Hawkes character in “Martha Marcy May Marlene.” She then honed in on the look of militias, always with an eye on the Houston locale. “The cowboy hat was crucial,” she said. “He needed something that didn’t just sit on his head, but was subtle. The costume was very much about the details, like the iconography of crosses on the jeans. John was still searching for who the character was, and when he stepped into the fitting room, he was transformed.”

Govan was particularly interested in how the character could use clothing to project authority and command attention. “I drew on Texas and Western iconography: the cowboy hat, boots, spurs, embellished denim, and prominent eye-catching details. The hat and boots give him an assertive, immediately recognizable silhouette. His outward display contrasts with the restraint of Latif’s everyday look.”

Hwan’s most arresting piece of clothing is a shirt he wears that Govan bought in a store but then completely embellished. “On a Friday evening I got a note, ‘Hey, we want to do some kind of portrait of his mother or something on the back of his shirt,'” Govan said. “This had to be on camera Monday, and we needed six multiples. I had to set about finding an airbrush artist who could hand paint and turn around some type of image of a mother in a very short amount of time, on top of embellishing the shirts.”

Fringe details and studs were added to the shirt’s placket and color, with everything coming together in a 72-hour period. “When you’re on a project like this, it’s a very short time frame,” Govan said, noting that she only had one fitting with each of her lead actors. Luckily, her extensive research and attention to detail paid off. “When we tried all the final pieces on that day and John stepped out of his camper fully loaded with the cowboy hat in his hand, the jeans, the shirt, the black ostrich boots with the spurs, and the belt buckle with crosses on it, it just came together.”

For the film’s third key character, Latif’s daughter Fatiha (Adia), Govan had to represent yet another approach to faith, with less latitude for overt stylization than in Latif or Pastor Hwan. “ Fatiha is somewhat wise beyond her years,” Govan said. “She’s finding herself. She’s trying to understand who she is as a young girl who has to grow up relatively quickly, and handle a lot of responsibility for her younger brother and her newly born sister. I wanted to show a young Muslim girl’s freedom of expression through her clothing.”

With that in mind, Govan’s research for Fatiha brought modest yet modern teenage silhouettes into conversation with roomy streetwear, track jackets, sports jerseys, sneakers, and expressive layering. One key to Govan’s approach was the way she handled the character’s hijabs. “Her colorful hijabs were tied and styled in various ways, giving her costumes a language of comfort and a controlled sense of teenage rebellion,” Govan said. “Her palette made room for rich mustard yellows, muted greens and blues, and lavender hues.”

Govan was also sure to use Fatiha’s look as a point of comparison and contrast with her father. “I wanted to portray the fact that she was youthful, she was vibrant, but she was also a rebel,” Govan said. “She was questioning her father in very direct ways, so it was important that she had an aesthetic that was very much her own. The color and silhouette gave her a different energy from her father while keeping her a formidable presence within the same grounded cultural world. Their costumes express different generations and points of view within the faith, community, and intimate family space they share.”

As with the other characters, Govan wanted Fatiha’s clothes to convey inner conflict. “There are moments where she’s just very pared down and very simple in the home,” Govan said, adding that one of her favorite looks comes in a scene where Fatiha steals milk for her baby sister. “She’s got this hockey jersey on, and she’s got her jeans, and she’s got her hijab, and it’s very freeing and vibrant. There’s a shot of her sitting in the mosque alone, and she’s observing, and she’s observing those around her. They’re in traditional dress, but she’s not. I wanted to show that juxtaposition.”

Govan credits her close collaborations not only with Tariq but also with the production designer, cinematographer, and other department heads for finding a cohesive vision for the film. “I knew that the palette that I was establishing would sit within their world,” Govan said. “I didn’t want the characters to stand outside it, and I didn’t want them to announce themselves. Everything was about balance, and that can’t happen alone. No costume designer, no cinematographer, no production designer is an island unto themselves. We work together, and we had a great collaboration.”

“Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother” is currently in theaters from Orion.
excerpt_original: Costume designer Deirdra Govan tells IndieWire about how meticulous research and cultural love led to costumes as expressive as they are beautiful.

article_text:
Archives – October 19, 2012

« Hi Sophie I applied to the Prix Virginia after seeing it in Le Journal and I just heard that I won with the Jones Family work! Crazy but it is a secret until the press are told on the 18th Oct! I am sitting in Chicago airport waiting for my connecting flight to Austin Texas and eating a massive frozen yoghurt, feeling slightly odd as its like 3am or something UK time. lovexxxx Liz »

Here’s the message that Liz sent a few weeks ago to tell me about her nomination for the Prix Virginia. Liz could be the reed in La Fontaine’s fable: it seems frail, falling, ready to collapse, but it resists with incredible force and stands up to the test of time. I met Liz more than ten years ago when I was an au pair at Oxford. Her simple message, sent from Austin, Texas, really touched me. It resembles her photographs. She exudes an overpowering essence of life that makes us believe that anything is possible. I wish her and the Jones family a nice trip!

Liz Hingley , 27, was born in Birmingham, UK. Le Journal published her work The Jones Family in May 2011 ( see here ). That same year, she received the Grants for Editorial Photography from Getty Images, and today she is the winner of the Prix Virginia, which gives her: – 10,000€ – A published portfolio in M, the magazine of Le Monde newspaper – An exhibition at the Hôtel de Sauroy from October 19 to November 30, 2012 (Tuesday to Saturday 2:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.)

Éditions be-pôles, publishers of the book collection Portraits de Villes , will give the winning photographer the carte blanche to photograph the city of his or her choice.
